title: Cephalus et Procris
titleEn: The Javelin and the Testing of Procris — Metamorphoses VII.661–758
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The day's talk ends, and next morning, with the east wind still holding the ships back, the Athenian envoys come to the king, who is still asleep; his son Phocus receives them and asks Cephalus about the javelin he carries — an unknown wood, a golden point, and, one of the brothers says, a weapon that strikes whatever it aims at and flies back bloodied with no one to fetch it. Cephalus will not say what it cost him, and weeps: soon after his marriage the dawn-goddess Aurora carried him off unwilling and sent him back in anger when he would speak of nothing but Procris; he then came home disguised to test his wife with gifts, made her waver at last, and lost her to the mountains and to Diana until his own confession brought her back. The javelin and a hound that outruns everything were her gifts on that return, and he ends by offering to tell what became of the other gift.

advisory.lede: The dawn-goddess Aurora carries Cephalus off against his will and keeps him for herself (704); the passage also names the carrying-off of Procris' sister Orithyia, and Cephalus calls his wife the worthier of the two to be seized.
advisory.more: Cephalus tells this himself. The second month after his marriage was running on when the goddess saw him setting nets on Hymettus at first light and took him — the Latin word is `invitum`, unwilling — and she let him go only after he would speak of nothing but his wife, and then in anger and with a prophecy against the marriage. What passed between them the poem does not narrate. The carrying-off of Orithyia by the north wind stands behind line 695 in a single participle, `raptae`, and Cephalus uses it to pay his wife a compliment: should Phocus set the two women side by side, he says, Procris was the one better worth seizing. The verb of seizing returns of Cephalus himself at 725, and in a compound at 732. The text is presented unaltered and the translations render what is there.

sentences.t:
Talibus atque aliis longum sermonibus illi
implevere diem.
sentences.l: With such conversations and with others they filled up the long day.
sentences.i: With talk of this kind and more besides they filled out the long day.
sentences.n: `implevere` is `impleverunt`, the poetic third-person plural perfect; `-ere` for `-erunt` is standard in verse. `talibus … sermonibus` opens and closes around `atque aliis`: Latin likes to begin a phrase, insert something, and only then finish it.

sentences.t:
Lucis pars ultima mensae
est data, nox somnis.
sentences.l: The last part of the daylight was given to the table, the night to sleep.
sentences.i: The last of the daylight went to the table, and the night to sleep.
sentences.n: `mensae` and `somnis` are datives — what each stretch of time was given to. `est data` serves both halves, and the second simply drops the verb. `lucis` here is daylight, not a lamp; `mensa` is the table and so the meal.

sentences.t:
Iubar aureus extulerat Sol
(flabat adhuc eurus redituraqua vela tenebat):
sentences.l: Golden Sol had lifted his beam (the east wind was still blowing, and it held the sails that were to return):
sentences.i: The golden Sun had raised his blaze — the east wind was still blowing, and it held back the sails that meant to sail home —
sentences.n: The Sun's rising marks the next morning. `eurus` is the east wind, which is keeping the Athenians' ships from setting out. The edition prints `redituraqua`, which is not a Latin word: the sentence needs `reditura-que`, the future participle `reditura` agreeing with `vela` plus the joining `-que`, and some editions print `redituraque`. The text is given here exactly as the edition has it.

sentences.t:
ad Cephalum Pallante sati, cui grandior aetas,
ad regem Cephalus simul et Pallante creati
conveniunt.
sentences.l: To Cephalus, to whom the greater age belonged, the men sown of Pallas come; to the king, Cephalus at the same time and the men fathered by Pallas.
sentences.i: The sons of Pallas came to Cephalus, who was the older; and Cephalus, together with the sons of Pallas, came to the king.
sentences.n: Two arrivals in one sentence, arranged so the pairs cross: the Pallantidae to Cephalus, then Cephalus and the Pallantidae to the king. `Pallante sati` and `Pallante creati` say the same thing in different words — 'sown of' and 'fathered by' Pallas — with the ablative of origin. `cui grandior aetas` is a dative of possession, 'to whom [was] the greater age', that is, he was the elder; the verb `conveniunt` is left to the end and covers both halves.

sentences.t: Sed adhuc regem sopor altus habebat.
sentences.l: But deep sleep still held the king.
sentences.i: But the king was still fast asleep.
sentences.n: Latin regularly makes the state the subject and the person its object: sleep holds the king rather than the king sleeping. `sopor` is heavy sleep, deeper than the `somnis` of 663.

sentences.t:
Excipit Aeacides illos in limine Phocus:
nam Telamon fraterque viros ad bella legebant.
sentences.l: Phocus, the son of Aeacus, receives them on the threshold: for Telamon and his brother were choosing men for the wars.
sentences.i: It was Phocus, Aeacus' son, who met them at the door, since Telamon and his brother were picking men for the war.
sentences.n: `Aeacides` — 'son of Aeacus' — is a patronymic, the standard way of naming a man by his father, and the name Phocus arrives only at the line's end, so the reader learns whose son before learning which one. The present `excipit` stands beside the imperfect `legebant`: the poem slips into the present to bring a scene close, not to change its time. The brother is not named here.

sentences.t:
Phocus in interius spatium pulchrosque recessus
Cecropidas ducit, cum quis simul ipse resedit.
sentences.l: Phocus leads the sons of Cecrops into an inner space and beautiful recesses, with whom he himself sat down at the same time.
sentences.i: Phocus led the Athenians into an inner room and its handsome recesses, and sat down there with them.
sentences.n: `Cecropidas` names the Athenians as descendants of Cecrops, their first king; the `-as` is a Greek accusative plural ending, kept because the word is Greek. `cum quis` is `cum quibus`, 'with whom': `quis` is an old ablative plural of the relative, not the interrogative 'who'.

sentences.t:
Adspicit Aeoliden ignota ex arbore factum
ferre manu iaculum, cuius fuit aurea cuspis.
sentences.l: He catches sight of the son of Aeolus carrying in his hand a javelin made from an unknown tree, whose point was golden.
sentences.i: He noticed the son of Aeolus carrying a javelin in his hand, made of a wood he did not know, and its point was gold.
sentences.n: `Aeoliden` is Cephalus, again by a patronymic — 'son of Aeolus'. `adspicit … ferre` is an accusative and infinitive: what Phocus sees is not the man but the man carrying. The edition's spelling `adspicit` for `aspicit` is its own and is kept.

sentences.t:
Pauca prius mediis sermonibus ille locutus
“sum nemorum studiosus” ait “caedisque ferinae:
sentences.l: He, having first spoken a few words in the middle of the conversation, says: 'I am a devotee of the woodlands and of the slaughter of wild beasts:
sentences.i: First he said a few words as the talk went on, and then: 'I am a lover of the woods and of hunting wild game.
sentences.n: `locutus` comes from the deponent `loquor`: passive in shape, active in sense, so 'having spoken', never 'having been spoken'. `studiosus` takes a genitive of what one is keen on, here two of them. `caedis ferinae` is literally 'the killing of beasts' — the ordinary Latin way of saying hunting.

sentences.t:
qua tamen e silva teneas hastile recisum,
iamdudum dubito.
sentences.l: yet from what wood you hold a shaft cut, I have long been in doubt.
sentences.i: but I have been wondering for a while now from what tree the shaft you hold was cut.
sentences.n: An indirect question — `qua e silva … recisum` — depends on `dubito`, which is why `teneas` is subjunctive; the question is folded inside the main clause and finished only at `dubito`. `iamdudum` with a present tense means something begun in the past and still going: 'I have been wondering for a while', not 'I wondered long ago'.

sentences.t:
Certe si fraxinus esset,
fulva colore foret; si cornus, nodus inesset.
sentences.l: Certainly, if it were ash, it would be tawny in colour; if cornel, a knot would be in it.
sentences.i: Certainly, if it were ash, it would be tawny; if cornel wood, it would have a knot in it.
sentences.n: Three imperfect subjunctives in a row — `esset`, `foret`, `inesset` — make unreal conditions, saying what the wood is not. `foret` is an alternative form of `esset`. `colore` is an ablative of respect: tawny in respect of its colour. Ash and cornel are the two woods a Roman would expect a spear-shaft to be cut from.

sentences.t:
Unde sit, ignoro. Sed non formosius isto
viderunt oculi telum iaculabile nostri.”
sentences.l: Where it is from, I do not know. But my eyes have not seen a more beautiful throwing-weapon than that of yours.
sentences.i: Where it comes from I cannot say. But my eyes have never seen a lovelier weapon to throw.
sentences.n: `unde sit` is another indirect question, again with the subjunctive. `isto` is an ablative of comparison after `formosius`, and `iste` points at what belongs to the person addressed — hence 'than that of yours'. `nostri` is the plural used for a singular, 'my', and it is held back to the very end of the line, far from the `oculi` it agrees with.

sentences.t:
Excipit Actaeis e fratribus alter, et “usum
maiorem specie mirabere” dixit “in isto.
sentences.l: One of the two Actaean brothers takes him up, and said: 'You will marvel at a usefulness greater than its look in that thing.
sentences.i: One of the two Athenian brothers took him up: 'What will astonish you in it is not how it looks but what it does.
sentences.n: `Actaeis` is 'of Acte', an old name for Attica, so another way of saying Athenian. `alter` is one of two, not merely 'another'. `specie` is an ablative of comparison after `maiorem`: its use is greater than its appearance. `mirabere` is `miraberis`, second-person singular future of the deponent `miror`, with the shortened ending that verse likes.

sentences.t:
Consequitur quodcumque petit, fortunaque missum
non regit, et revolat nullo referente cruentum.”
sentences.l: It overtakes whatever it seeks, and chance does not steer it once thrown, and it flies back bloodied with no one bringing it back.
sentences.i: It catches whatever it aims at; luck has no hand in its flight; and it comes back bloody with no one to carry it.
sentences.n: `nullo referente` is an ablative absolute, a self-contained 'with nobody bringing it back' where English wants a whole clause. `missum` is a participle doing similar work: 'once it has been thrown'. `consequitur` is deponent — active in sense despite its passive shape — and `cruentum` agrees with the weapon, so the blood is on it as it returns.

sentences.t:
Tum vero iuvenis Nereius omnia quaerit,
cur sit et unde datum, quis tanti muneris auctor.
sentences.l: Then indeed the Nereian youth asks everything: why and from where it was given, who the giver of so great a gift was.
sentences.i: Then the young grandson of Nereus asked it all — why the gift was made, where it came from, who gave so great a present.
sentences.n: `Nereius` marks Phocus as descended from Nereus, an old god of the sea, through his mother; one adjective does the work of a whole clause. Three indirect questions hang from `quaerit`, and the third drops its verb entirely — 'who [was] the author of so great a gift'. `datum` is neuter, agreeing with the unspoken `telum`.

sentences.t:
Quae petit, ille refert. Sed enim (narrare pudori est !),
qua tulerit mercede silet;
sentences.l: The things which he asks, that man tells. But indeed — to tell is a thing for shame! — at what price he got it he keeps silent;
sentences.i: He told him what he asked. But — it shames him to tell — he says nothing about the price he paid for it;
sentences.n: `quae petit` is a connecting relative used as the object: 'the things which he asks'. `pudori est` is a predicative dative, literally 'is for a shame', the ordinary Latin for 'brings shame'. `qua … mercede` is an indirect question split around its own verb, which is why `tulerit` is subjunctive. The line quietly warns that something in the story ahead does the teller no credit.

sentences.t:
tactusque dolore
coniugis amissae lacrimis ita fatur obortis:
sentences.l: and, touched by grief for his lost wife, with tears having welled up, he speaks thus:
sentences.i: and, stirred by grief for the wife he had lost, he began to speak with the tears rising:
sentences.n: `lacrimis … obortis` is an ablative absolute wrapped around the rest of the clause: 'with tears having sprung up'. `fatur` is deponent and active in sense, 'he speaks'. `coniugis amissae` is the wife the grief is for — the poem gives away her fate before it has told her story.

sentences.t:
“Hoc me, nate dea, (quis possit credere?) telum
flere facit facietque diu, si vivere nobis
fata diu dederint.
sentences.l: This weapon, you born of a goddess — who could believe it? — makes me weep and will make me weep long, if the fates shall have granted us to live long.
sentences.i: Son of a goddess — who could believe it? — this weapon makes me weep, and will go on making me weep, if the fates grant me a long life.
sentences.n: `nate dea` is a vocative with an ablative of origin, 'you born of a goddess'. `hoc … telum` is split across the whole line, so the reader hears 'this' long before learning what 'this' is. `quis possit credere` is a potential subjunctive — 'who could believe?' `dederint` is future perfect, and `nobis` is plural for singular, 'me'.

sentences.t:
Hoc me cum coniuge cara
perdidit: hoc utinam caruissem munere semper!
sentences.l: This destroyed me along with my dear wife: this gift — would that I had always lacked it!
sentences.i: This is what ruined me, and my dear wife with me. If only I had never had this gift at all!
sentences.n: `careo` takes an ablative of the thing lacked, so `hoc … munere` is 'of this gift'. `utinam` with a pluperfect subjunctive makes a wish about the past that can no longer be met — regret, not hope. `hoc` opens both halves of the sentence, one word carrying the weight twice.

sentences.t:
Procris erat (si forte magis pervenit ad aures
Orithyia tuas, raptae soror Orithyiae),
sentences.l: There was Procris — if by chance Orithyia has reached your ears more, the sister of the seized Orithyia —
sentences.i: There was Procris — sister of Orithyia, if Orithyia's name has come to you the better known, the Orithyia who was carried off —
sentences.n: `raptae` is the perfect participle of `rapio`, 'seized, carried off': Orithyia was taken by force by Boreas, the north wind, and one word is all the poem spends on it here. `ad aures … tuas` is split around the name, so Orithyia sits inside 'your ears'. `magis` is comparative: the sister is the better known of the two.

sentences.t:
si faciem moresque velis conferre duarum,
dignior ipsa rapi.
sentences.l: if you should wish to compare the face and character of the two, she herself was worthier to be seized.
sentences.i: if you cared to set the two women's looks and character side by side, she was the one better worth seizing.
sentences.n: `rapi` is the passive infinitive of `rapio` after `dignior`: worthier to be carried off. Cephalus praises his wife in the only terms her sister's story supplies, and those terms are abduction — the compliment and the violence are the same sentence. The verb of this sentence is the `erat` of 694, before the parenthesis: 'Procris was … herself worthier to be seized'. `velis` is a potential subjunctive, 'should you wish'; `duarum` is a genitive with `faciem moresque`, held back to the end of its line.

sentences.t:
Pater hanc mihi iunxit Erechtheus,
hanc mihi iunxit amor.
sentences.l: Her father Erechtheus joined her to me; love joined her to me.
sentences.i: Her father Erechtheus gave her to me in marriage; love gave her to me as well.
sentences.n: The same three words return, `hanc mihi iunxit`, with only the subject changed: the legal match and the loved one are set side by side and weighed against each other. `iungo` is the ordinary verb for making a marriage, and using it twice makes the second joining as binding as the first.

sentences.t:
Felix dicebar eramque.
Non ita dis visum est, aut nunc quoque forsitan essem.
sentences.l: I was called happy, and I was. It did not so seem to the gods — or now too I would perhaps be.
sentences.i: I was called a happy man, and I was one. The gods did not see it that way; otherwise I might be happy still.
sentences.n: `dis visum est` — 'it seemed good to the gods' — is the standard Latin for a decision taken above, with `dis` the dative plural of `deus`. `dicebar` is a true passive, 'I was being called'. `forsitan`, 'perhaps', regularly takes the subjunctive, and `essem` is also the 'then' half of an unreal condition whose 'if' half is never stated: `aut` carries it alone, 'or else I would be'.

sentences.t:
Alter agebatur post sacra iugalia mensis,
cum me cornigeris tendentem retia cervis
vertice de summo semper florentis Hymetti
lutea mane videt pulsis Aurora tenebris
sentences.l: The second month after the marriage rites was being passed, when saffron Aurora, the shadows having been driven off, sees me in the morning stretching nets for the horned stags from the highest peak of ever-flowering Hymettus,
sentences.i: The second month after our wedding was running on, when saffron Dawn, the darkness once driven back, saw me in the morning setting nets for the antlered deer on the topmost ridge of Hymettus, which flowers all year,
sentences.n: `cum … videt` is the inverted `cum`: the main event of the sentence arrives inside the `cum` clause, and the present tense drops you into it. `pulsis … tenebris` is an ablative absolute, 'with the shadows driven off' — daybreak stated as a fact about the sky. `cornigeris … cervis` is a dative: the nets are set for the stags. `lutea` is the saffron-yellow of first light, and Aurora is that light as well as a goddess, so the colour word works twice. Hymettus is the mountain south-east of Athens.

sentences.t:
invitumque rapit. Liceat mihi vera referre
pace deae.
sentences.l: and carries me off unwilling. May it be permitted me to report true things, by the goddess's leave.
sentences.i: and carried me off against my will. Let me be allowed to tell the truth, with the goddess's pardon.
sentences.n: `invitum` is a single accusative adjective agreeing with `me`, and it carries the whole weight of the sentence: he was taken unwilling. `rapit` is the same verb used of Orithyia a few lines earlier (695). `pace deae` is an ablative of attendant circumstance — 'with the goddess's peace' — a set phrase for saying something risky about a god without giving offence. `liceat` is a jussive subjunctive.

sentences.t:
Quod sit roseo spectabilis ore,
quod teneat lucis, teneat confinia noctis,
nectareis quod alatur aquis, ego —Procrin amabam:
sentences.l: Although she is worth looking at in her rosy face, although she holds the borders of light, holds the borders of night, although she is nourished on nectar-waters — I loved Procris:
sentences.i: Granted she is lovely to look at, with her rosy face; granted she holds the boundary of the day and the boundary of the night; granted her food is nectar-streams — I loved Procris.
sentences.n: Three `quod` clauses with the subjunctive, all concessive: 'granted that …'. They pile up the goddess's beauties only so that the last three words can set them aside. `teneat lucis, teneat confinia noctis` splits one phrase into two by repeating the verb: she holds the border where day begins and the border where night does. `ore` is an ablative of respect, 'in respect of her face'; `alatur` is passive, 'she is fed'. `Procrin` keeps its Greek accusative ending. The `ego` is broken off — the dash is the edition's — and the sentence lands instead on the plainest words it has, `Procrin amabam`.

sentences.t: pectore Procris erat, Procris mihi semper in ore.
sentences.l: In my breast Procris was, Procris always on the lips to me.
sentences.i: Procris was in my heart; Procris was always on my lips.
sentences.n: `pectore` and `in ore` are the ordinary Latin pair for what one feels and what one says. `mihi` is a dative of possession — 'on the lips to me' — where English simply wants 'my'. The name stands twice, once in each half of the line, at the same weight; and `ore`, which three lines earlier was the goddess's face (705), is here Cephalus' own mouth.

sentences.t:
Sacra tori coitusque novos thalamosque recentes
primaque deserti referebam foedera lecti.
sentences.l: The rites of the marriage-bed and our new couplings and the fresh bridal chambers and the first bonds of the deserted bed I kept bringing up.
sentences.i: I kept speaking of our marriage rites, our new-made union, the bridal chamber still fresh, the first vows of the bed I had left behind.
sentences.n: Four objects heaped up with `-que … -que … -que`, each a different name for the same marriage, which is named four times over and in different words each time. `referebam` is imperfect, so he said it over and over. `deserti … lecti` wraps around the other words, and the participle quietly admits whose absence it was.

sentences.t:
Mota dea est et “siste tuas, ingrate, querellas:
Procrin habe!” dixit.
sentences.l: The goddess was moved, and said: 'Stop your complaints, ungrateful man: have Procris!'
sentences.i: The goddess was stirred, and said: 'Stop your whining, ungrateful man — have your Procris!'
sentences.n: `mota … est` is a true passive, 'she was moved', and what moves her is at least as much anger as pity. `ingrate` is a vocative thrown into the middle of her command. `siste` and `habe` are both imperatives, and the second is given as a curse rather than a favour. `querellas` is the edition's spelling of `querelas`.

sentences.t:
“Quodsi mea provida mens est,
non habuisse voles.”
sentences.l: But if my mind is far-seeing, you will wish not to have had her.
sentences.i: But if my mind sees ahead, you will wish you had never had her.
sentences.n: `quodsi` is 'but if'. `non habuisse voles` sets a future beside a perfect infinitive: the wishing lies ahead, the thing to be unwished is already done. A goddess is not guessing when she says this — the condition is a prophecy in disguise, and the whole of what follows is its working out.

sentences.t:
Meque illi irata remisit.
Dum redeo mecumque deae memorata retracto,
sentences.l: And, angry, she sent me back to her. While I return and turn over with myself the things the goddess had said,
sentences.i: And in anger she sent me back to Procris. On the way home, going over to myself what the goddess had said,
sentences.n: `irata` is a nominative adjective agreeing with the goddess: her anger is stated in one word and dropped. `illi` is a dative, 'to her' — to Procris, who has not been named for several lines. `memorata` is a neuter plural participle used as a noun, 'the things spoken'; `retracto` is to handle a thing again, and so to turn it over in the mind. Magnus prints `Dum`, 'while'; some editions print `cum`, 'when'.

sentences.t:
esse metus coepit, ne iura iugalia coniunx
non bene servasset.
sentences.l: a fear began to be, that my wife had not kept the marriage rights well.
sentences.i: a fear began to take shape: that my wife had not kept her marriage vows as she should.
sentences.n: After a word of fearing, `ne` marks the thing feared and is not itself a negative in English; the `non` is the real negative, so what he fears is that she had *not* kept them. `servasset` is the shortened `servavisset`, pluperfect subjunctive. `esse … coepit`, 'began to be', is heavier than 'arose' and holds the fear at arm's length for a moment.

sentences.t:
Facies aetasque iubebat
credere adulterium; prohibebant credere mores.
sentences.l: Her beauty and her youth ordered me to believe adultery; her character forbade me to believe it.
sentences.i: Her looks and her youth told me to believe in adultery; her character forbade the belief.
sentences.n: The two halves are set back to front: subject then verb in the first, verb then subject in the second, with `credere` repeated in each and only the verb changed from ordering to forbidding. `facies` is the face and so her beauty; `aetas` her age, meaning she was young. `mores` is settled character, a person's way of being, not manners.

sentences.t:
Sed tamen afueram, sed et haec erat unde redibam,
criminis exemplum, sed cuncta timemus amantes.
sentences.l: But still I had been away; but this woman too, the one I was returning from, was an example of the crime; but we lovers fear everything.
sentences.i: But still — I had been away; and she I was coming back from was herself a case of the very offence; but we who love fear everything.
sentences.n: Three clauses each opening with `sed`, the argument stumbling forward against itself. `haec` is feminine and points at Aurora herself, and `unde` here is 'from whom', not 'from where': the goddess he has just come back from was `criminis exemplum`, a specimen of the very offence he now suspects, and the phrase naming it is held over to the next line. `amantes` is a participle used as a noun, standing in apposition to the 'we' inside `timemus`.

sentences.t:
Quaerere quod doleam statuo donisque pudicam
sollicitare fidem.
sentences.l: I decide to look for something at which I may grieve, and to work on her chaste faith with gifts.
sentences.i: I resolved to go looking for something that would hurt me, and to tempt her chaste loyalty with presents.
sentences.n: `quod doleam` is a relative clause of purpose, with the subjunctive: something he might grieve at. He is not fearing a wound, he is going to find one. `sollicitare` is to shake or unsettle, and used of loyalty it means to try to corrupt it. Both infinitives depend on `statuo`, which sits between them.

sentences.t:
Favet huic Aurora timori
inmutatque meam (videor sensisse) figuram.
sentences.l: Aurora favours this fear and changes my shape — I seem to have felt it.
sentences.i: Aurora encouraged this fear of mine and altered my appearance — I think I felt it happen.
sentences.n: `faveo` takes a dative, so `huic … timori` is what she is favouring: the goddess is on the side of the suspicion, not of the marriage. `videor sensisse` is the personal use of `videor` — 'I seem to have felt' — where English prefers 'it seems that I felt'; Latin makes the speaker the subject. The edition's `inmutat` for `immutat` is its own spelling and is kept.

sentences.t:
Palladias ineo non cognoscendus Athenas
ingrediorque domum.
sentences.l: I enter Pallas' Athens, not to be recognised, and I go into the house.
sentences.i: I entered Athens, the city of Pallas, in a shape no one could know, and went into my own house.
sentences.n: `non cognoscendus` is a gerundive used as an adjective of the speaker: 'not to be recognised', that is, unrecognisable. Athens is `Palladias` because Pallas Athena is its patron, and the adjective stands in for the whole story of the city's naming. `ingredior` is deponent — passive in form, active in sense.

sentences.t:
Culpa domus ipsa carebat
castaque signa dabat dominoque erat anxia rapto:
sentences.l: The house itself lacked fault and was giving chaste signs and was anxious for its master, who had been carried off:
sentences.i: The house itself was free of fault: everything in it spoke of chastity, and it was full of anxiety for the master who had been seized:
sentences.n: `careo` again takes an ablative of the thing lacking, `culpa`. `domino … rapto` is the verb of seizing once more, this time of Cephalus himself — the household is still grieving an abduction. `anxia` with a dative is 'anxious for'. Ovid gives the wife's character to the building and lets the house testify in her place.

sentences.t: vix aditus per mille dolos ad Erechthida factus.
sentences.l: scarcely was an approach made to the daughter of Erechtheus, through a thousand tricks.
sentences.i: Only by a thousand tricks was it possible to get near Erechtheus' daughter at all.
sentences.n: `aditus … factus` has no verb printed: `est` is left for the reader to supply, as Latin often does with a perfect passive. `mille` is not a count but the ordinary Latin for 'countless'. `Erechthida` is a Greek accusative patronymic, 'the daughter of Erechtheus' — Procris, named by her father as she was at line 697.

sentences.t:
Ut vidi, obstipui meditataque paene reliqui
temptamenta fide.
sentences.l: When I saw her, I was struck dumb, and I almost abandoned the trials of her faith that I had planned.
sentences.i: The moment I saw her I was struck dumb, and I nearly gave up the test of her loyalty I had rehearsed.
sentences.n: `ut` with the perfect indicative is 'when, as soon as'. `fide` is an old genitive singular of `fides`, 'of her faith', not an ablative — the trials belong to her loyalty. `meditata`, from the deponent `meditor`, 'plan, rehearse', agrees with `temptamenta` and is used passively here: the tests he had worked out beforehand.

sentences.t:
Male me, quin vera faterer,
continui, male, quin, ut oportuit, oscula ferrem.
sentences.l: Badly I held myself back from confessing the truth, badly from bringing kisses, as was fitting.
sentences.i: It was all I could do to keep from telling her the truth, all I could do to keep from kissing her as I should have.
sentences.n: `quin` with the subjunctive after a verb of restraining means 'from doing': `continui quin faterer` is 'I held myself back from confessing'. `male continui` is 'I restrained myself badly', that is, only just. `oportuit` is impersonal, 'it was fitting'. The doubled `male` is the whole cost of the plan, admitted in one word twice.

sentences.t:
Tristis erat (sed nulla tamen formosior illa
esse potest tristi) desiderioque calebat
coniugis abrepti.
sentences.l: She was sad — yet no woman can be more beautiful than she, sad — and she was burning with longing for the husband snatched away.
sentences.i: She was grieving — and no woman can be lovelier than she is in grief — and she was hot with longing for the husband who had been carried off.
sentences.n: `illa … tristi` is an ablative of comparison with its adjective attached, so the comparison is not with her but with her in that state. `coniugis abrepti` is the verb of seizing again, now in a compound and now in Procris' own understanding of what happened to Cephalus. Magnus prints `calebat`, 'was warm, glowed' — the word for physical heat used of longing; some editions print `dolebat`, 'was in pain'.

sentences.t:
Tu conlige, qualis in illa,
Phoce, decor fuerit, quam sic dolor ipse decebat.
sentences.l: Gather it yourself, Phocus — what beauty was in her, whom grief itself so became.
sentences.i: Judge for yourself, Phocus, what beauty she had, when grief itself so suited her.
sentences.n: `conlige` is an imperative, 'draw the conclusion' (the edition's spelling of `collige`). `qualis … fuerit` is an indirect question, hence the subjunctive. `decet` takes an accusative of the person a thing suits, so `quam` is its object and `dolor` its subject: grief became her, not she it. `Phoce` is a vocative — the speaker turns aside from the story to address his listener, and the turn is a way of asking to be believed.

sentences.t:
Quid referam, quotiens temptamina nostra pudici
reppulerint mores, quotiens “ego” dixerit “uni
servor; ubicumque est, uni mea gaudia servo!”
sentences.l: Why should I report how often her chaste character drove back my attempts, how often she said: 'I am kept for one man; wherever he is, I keep my joys for one man!'
sentences.i: Why should I tell how often her chaste character threw back my attempts, how often she said: 'I am kept for one man alone; wherever he is, it is for him alone that I keep my joys.'
sentences.n: `quid referam` is a deliberative subjunctive, 'why should I tell?' — a way of passing over what he does not wish to dwell on while telling it anyway. `reppulerint` and `dixerit` are subjunctive because `quotiens` makes indirect questions. `servor` is passive, 'I am kept', and `servo` active, 'I keep': she says the same thing twice over, once as something done to her and once as something she does. `uni` is a dative, 'for one man'.

sentences.t:
Cui non ista fide satis experientia sano
magna foret?
sentences.l: To what man in his right mind would that trial of her faith not be large enough?
sentences.i: What man in his senses would not have found that test of her loyalty enough?
sentences.n: `cui … sano` is a dative with `foret`, 'for whom, being sound of mind' — and the adjective quietly concedes that he was not. `fide` is again the old genitive of `fides`, as at 728. `satis magna` is split around `experientia`. `foret` stands for `esset`, here in an unreal condition with no 'if' clause.

sentences.t:
Non sum contentus et in mea pugno
vulnera, dum census dare me pro nocte loquendo
muneraque augendo tandem dubitare coegi.
sentences.l: I am not content, and I fight into my own wounds, until, by saying that I would give my whole fortune for one night and by increasing the gifts, I at last forced her to hesitate.
sentences.i: I was not satisfied; I fought my way toward my own wounding, until, by offering my entire estate for a single night and by piling the presents higher, I made her waver at last.
sentences.n: `in mea pugno vulnera` is 'I fight into my own wounds' — the wound is what he is fighting to reach, not what he is fighting against, and the phrase is his own verdict on himself. `loquendo` and `augendo` are ablative gerunds, 'by saying' and 'by increasing', the ordinary Latin way of naming the means. `census` is a man's whole assessed property. The present tenses `sum` and `pugno` sit inside a past story: the narrative speeds up as it nears the break.

sentences.t:
Exclamo: “Male (fictor adest !), male fictus adulter
verus eram coniunx! me, perfida, teste teneris!”
sentences.l: I cry out: 'Wickedly — the pretender is here! — wickedly a feigned adulterer, I was your true husband! You are caught, faithless woman, with me as witness!'
sentences.i: I cried out: 'The pretender stands here! To my own ruin I played the adulterer — I was your true husband. You are caught, faithless woman, and I am the witness against you.'
sentences.n: The line is a knot: `fictus adulter` and `verus coniunx` are both said of the same 'I', and the false lover and the real husband turn out to be one man. `male` twice, once with the parenthesis and once with `fictus`, is 'wickedly' and also 'to his own cost'. `me … teste` is an ablative absolute, 'with me as witness', wrapped around the vocative `perfida`. Magnus prints `fictor adest`, 'the pretender is here'; some editions print `victor`, 'the winner'.

sentences.t:
Illa nihil. Tacito tantummodo victa pudore
insidiosa malo cum coniuge limina fugit;
sentences.l: She, nothing. Overcome only by a silent shame, she fled the treacherous threshold, and the wicked husband along with it;
sentences.i: She said nothing. Beaten only by a silent shame, she fled the house that had set the trap, and her bad husband with it;
sentences.n: `illa nihil` has no verb at all — her silence is written into the grammar as a gap. `victa` is a true passive participle, 'having been overcome'. `insidiosa … limina` is the doorway that laid the ambush, the adjective moved from the man to the place he stood in. `malo cum coniuge` puts the preposition between adjective and noun, which is normal in verse; the husband is part of what she flees, not her companion in flight.

sentences.t:
offensaque mei genus omne perosa virorum
montibus errabat, studiis operata Dianae.
sentences.l: and, offended at me, hating the whole race of men, she wandered in the mountains, engaged in the pursuits of Diana.
sentences.i: and, wounded by me and loathing the whole race of men, she roamed the mountains, given over to Diana's pursuits.
sentences.n: `perosa` is a perfect participle with a present and active sense, 'hating', from `perodi`, a verb that exists only in its perfect tenses. `genus omne … virorum` is split around it. `operata` with `studiis` is 'occupied in, devoted to'. Diana is the huntress and a virgin goddess, so her `studia` say both where Procris went and what she was giving up, in one phrase.

sentences.t:
Tum mihi deserto violentior ignis ad ossa
pervenit.
sentences.l: Then, to me abandoned, a more violent fire reached to the bones.
sentences.i: Then, left alone, I felt a fiercer fire reach the bone.
sentences.n: `mihi deserto` is a dative of the person affected: the fire comes to him, deserted. `violentior` is comparative with nothing named to compare against — fiercer than it had been before he drove her off. `ad ossa` is where Latin puts a feeling that goes all the way down.

sentences.t:
Orabam veniam et peccasse fatebar
et potuisse datis simili succumbere culpae
me quoque muneribus, si munera tanta darentur.
sentences.l: I kept begging pardon and admitted that I had done wrong, and that I too could have sunk under a like fault, with such gifts given, if gifts so great were offered.
sentences.i: I begged her pardon; I admitted I had done wrong, and that I too could have fallen into the same fault, had presents on that scale been offered me.
sentences.n: Two accusative-and-infinitive clauses hang from `fatebar` — `peccasse` (short for `peccavisse`) and `potuisse` — and their shared subject `me` is held back to the last line. `datis … muneribus` is an ablative absolute wrapped around the clause, 'gifts having been given'. `simili … culpae` is a dative with `succumbere`, to give way to. `si … darentur` is an unreal condition, so the confession costs him nothing that is real.

sentences.t:
Haec mihi confesso, laesum prius ulta pudorem,
redditur et dulces concorditer exigit annos.
sentences.l: To me, having confessed these things, she is given back, having first avenged her injured modesty, and she spends sweet years in concord.
sentences.i: When I had confessed all this she was given back to me — she had first avenged the shame done to her — and we passed sweet years in harmony.
sentences.n: `mihi confesso` is a dative with the perfect participle of the deponent `confiteor`, active in sense: 'to me, having confessed', with `haec` as its object. `ulta` is likewise a deponent participle with active force, 'having avenged'; what she avenged was `laesum … pudorem`, the modesty he had injured, and her flight to the mountains was the revenge. `redditur` is passive, 'she is given back', so that the reconciliation is stated as something that happens to him.

sentences.t:
Dat mihi praeterea, tamquam se parva dedisset
dona, canem munus, quem cum sua traderet illi
Cynthia, “currendo superabit” dixerat “omnes.”
sentences.l: She gives me besides — as though in giving herself she had given small gifts — a dog as a present, of which, when her own Cynthia was handing it over to her, she had said: 'It will surpass all others by running.'
sentences.i: She gave me besides — as though in giving herself she had given only a small thing — a hound for a present, of which Cynthia, when she handed it to her, had said: 'It will outrun them all.'
sentences.n: `tamquam … dedisset` is an unreal comparison with the pluperfect subjunctive, 'as if she had given'. Cynthia is Diana, named from Mount Cynthus on Delos, her birthplace — a cult title standing in for the name, and `sua` marks her as the goddess Procris had been serving in the mountains. `currendo` is an ablative gerund, 'by running'. `quem` is pulled to the head of its clause, in front of the `cum` clause it encloses, where English has to unpack it as 'of which'.

sentences.t: Dat simul et iaculum, manibus quod (cernis) habemus.
sentences.l: She gives at the same time the javelin too, which — you see it — we hold in our hands.
sentences.i: At the same time she gave me the javelin as well, the one you see here in my hands.
sentences.n: `habemus` is a plural used for a singular, 'I hold', and `manibus` need not mean both hands. `cernis` is dropped in as a parenthesis, so the story turns for a moment back to the object Phocus asked about at the start (672-673). The question about where the javelin came from has now been answered; the price named at 688 is still unspoken.

sentences.t:
Muneris alterius quae sit fortuna, requiris?
Accipe mirandum: novitate movebere facti.
sentences.l: What the fortune of the other gift is, you ask? Take in a thing to be wondered at: you will be moved by the newness of the deed.
sentences.i: Do you ask what became of the other gift? Then hear something to marvel at: the strangeness of what happened will move you.
sentences.n: `muneris alterius` is a genitive pulled in front of the question word it belongs to; `alterius` is 'the other' of the two gifts — the hound, since the javelin is already in his hand. `quae sit` is an indirect question, hence the subjunctive. `mirandum` is a gerundive used as a noun, 'a thing that must be wondered at'. `movebere` is `moveberis`, second-person singular future passive — 'you will be moved' — with the same shortened ending as `mirabere` at 682.
